opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where knowledge actually comes from. If you look at how we built vision systems for most of the last decade, the recipe was supervised learning: you collect millions of images, you pay people to label them, "this is a dog," "this is a car," and the model learns to map pixels to those labels. That works remarkably well for the task you defined. But the labels are a very thin slice of what's actually in the image. A human annotator writes "dog," but the image also contains the lighting, the geometry of the room, the fact that the dog is sitting on a couch and not floating in the air, that the couch is soft, that the shadow falls a certain way. None of that is in the label, so the model has no incentive to learn it.

Common sense, to me, is exactly that unlabeled stuff. It's the huge body of implicit knowledge about how the world is structured: objects persist, things fall down, surfaces support other things, parts belong to wholes. Nobody teaches a baby these things with flashcards. A child just looks at the world, interacts with it, predicts what will happen next, and gets surprised when the prediction is wrong. That surprise signal comes from the data itself, not from a teacher.

Self-supervised learning is our attempt to give machines that same kind of signal. You hide part of the input and ask the model to fill it in, or you show two views of the same scene and ask the model to recognize they're the same thing, or you ask it to predict the next frame. The supervision is derived from the structure of the data. And to do well on those tasks, the model is forced to internalize regularities about the world, because that's the only way to make good predictions. You can't fill in a masked region of a face convincingly unless you've learned something about faces.

The other part is scale. Labels are expensive and they're bounded by human effort and by human vocabulary. Raw visual data, images and especially video, is essentially unlimited. So if you want a system that has absorbed the long tail of how the world works, the only realistic path is to learn from the data directly without waiting for someone to annotate it.

I'll add one caveat, because I think it matters. Self-supervised learning on its own isn't a magic ticket to common sense. A lot of current methods still learn representations that are very good for recognition but not necessarily for physical reasoning or for planning. Language models showed us that predicting the next token at scale can produce something surprisingly general, and in vision we're still searching for the equivalent objective, one that's rich enough to capture the world rather than just texture and appearance. So I see self-supervision as the right principle, learning from the world itself, but I think we're still early in figuring out the right form of it, especially as we move toward video, 3D, and agents that actually act in the environment. That's what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says labels capture only a thin slice of an image and give models no incentive to learn the rest, framing labeled learning as insufficient for common sense.

r002.rationale: It describes hiding part of an input and asking the model to fill it in, with supervision derived from the data’s structure rather than human annotation.

r003.rationale: It says masked-region prediction requires learning about faces and world regularities, but does not state that humans use physical-world understanding to infer missing or corrupted visual information as the rationale for these objectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the starting point is a simple observation about how humans learn. A baby doesn't come into the world with labeled data. Nobody tells a one-year-old "this is a cat, this is a chair, this object is occluded by that one." The child just watches, moves around, pokes at things, and over time builds up an understanding of how the world works. Objects persist when they go out of view. Things fall when you drop them. Surfaces have textures and depth. That's what we loosely call common sense, and almost none of it comes from explicit supervision.

Now look at how we've historically trained vision systems. We take millions of images, we pay people to attach a word to each one, and we train a network to predict that word. It works remarkably well for the specific task, but it's a very narrow signal. The label "dog" tells you almost nothing about the fur, the shadow, the ground, the fact that the dog is standing on grass and the grass is attached to the earth. Most of the information in the image is simply thrown away because it's not relevant to the classification objective. So you end up with a model that's very good at matching textures to categories but doesn't really understand the scene.

Self-supervised learning flips this around. Instead of asking "what's the name of this thing," you ask the model to learn from the structure of the data itself. Predict the missing part of an image. Figure out that two different crops of the same photo belong together. Predict what the next frame of a video looks like. These objectives force the model to capture much richer information, because you can't fill in a masked region or predict motion without implicitly learning something about shape, depth, physical continuity, how parts relate to wholes. In a sense, the supervision signal is the world itself, and the world is a much more generous teacher than a human annotator.

The other reason I find this compelling is scale. Common sense is broad by definition. You can't enumerate it as a set of labeled tasks. But visual data is essentially unlimited. Every camera, every video on the internet, is a potential training signal. If the learning objective is grounded in the data rather than in human annotation, you can keep pushing the amount of experience the model has, and that's really the only path I see toward something that generalizes the way a child's understanding generalizes.

I want to be honest that we're not there yet. Current self-supervised models learn very good representations, but there's still a gap between "good features for downstream tasks" and genuine understanding of how the physical world behaves. Part of that is probably the modality: static images only tell you so much, and I think video, and eventually interaction, will matter a lot more. But directionally, I'm fairly convinced. If you want a vision system to have common sense, it has to be able to learn from observing the world without someone standing over it with a label for every pixel.

r001.rationale: The response says labeled-image training provides a narrow signal and that most scene information is discarded, leaving models without real scene understanding. It presents learning beyond human labels as necessary for common sense.

r003.rationale: The response says self-supervised prediction tasks can teach models about shape, depth, and physical continuity. It does not state that humans rely on physical-world understanding to infer missing or corrupted visual information as the rationale for those tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that common sense is very difficult to capture with a fixed set of labels. If you train a vision system only to recognize categories, you’re telling it, “This is a dog; this is a chair.” But understanding the visual world involves much more: how objects relate to one another, what happens when something moves, what you should expect to see next.

Self-supervised learning gives us a way to learn some of that structure from the data itself. For example, if a model has to predict a missing part of an image or what comes next in a video, it needs to discover regularities in the world without someone explicitly annotating every one of them. That’s an appealing direction because humans also learn so much through observation, beyond what we’re directly taught.

But I would be careful about saying that self-supervised learning automatically produces common sense. A model can become very good at prediction by exploiting patterns that don’t generalize. The hope is that these learning objectives can build a foundation—and then we need to test whether the system can actually use what it has learned in unfamiliar situations.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting a missing image part or what comes next in a video, but does not explain that a known image transformation supplies the target.

r003.rationale: It mentions human learning through observation and models predicting missing content, but does not connect the objectives to humans using physical-world understanding to infer missing or corrupted visual information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of common sense is knowledge that we acquire without anyone explicitly teaching us. We observe the world, we interact with it, and we gradually learn what tends to happen. Objects persist when they disappear behind something. Things move in particular ways. Nobody needs to label every instance of those experiences for us.

Self-supervised learning offers a way to learn from that kind of observation. Instead of asking a model only to recognize a category that a human has annotated, we ask it to learn relationships within the data itself—for example, to predict missing information or what might happen next in a video. To do that well, the model may need to discover something about objects, motion, and the structure of a scene.

But I would distinguish learning useful representations from actually having common sense. A system can become very good at a prediction task by exploiting patterns that don’t reflect a deep understanding of the world. So self-supervised learning is a promising foundation, rather than a guarantee. The interesting question is how to make the learning process capture the kinds of knowledge that generalize to unfamiliar situations.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts self-supervised learning with recognizing human-annotated categories, but does not state that labeled data alone is insufficient for computer-vision systems to acquire common sense.

r002.rationale: It mentions predicting missing information as an example, but does not describe applying a known transformation to an image to create an unannotated prediction target.

r003.rationale: It says prediction may reveal objects, motion, and scene structure, but does not explain that humans use physical-world understanding to infer missing or corrupted visual information.
